overview.summary: Who decides which lawful but harmful posts stay online — platforms, governments, courts, or users — and whether the liability shield behind the social web should hold.
overview.scope_covered: Moderation of lawful-but-harmful speech: liability shields, duty-of-care mandates, transparency and appeals, must-carry rules, state pressure, age gating.
overview.scope_excluded: Already-illegal content enforcement, copyright takedowns, AI deepfake rules, and broader antitrust or privacy regulation of platforms.
overview.why_now: In March 2026 juries in Los Angeles and New Mexico held Meta liable for design and algorithm harms on a product-defect theory that never reached its Section 230 defense, teeing up the shield’s first real test on appeal.

stats.label: Section 230’s age · enacted 1996
stats.note: The 1996 shield protects platforms from publisher liability for user posts — written years before today’s major platforms existed.
stats.detail: The shield already carries carve-outs: federal crimes, intellectual-property claims, wiretapping and privacy claims, and, since FOSTA-SESTA in 2018, civil claims tied to sex trafficking. Defenders often cite a 2017 NERA Economic Consulting estimate crediting Section 230 and the DMCA with roughly 425,000 US jobs and $44 billion a year — a dated, industry-funded figure rather than an independent current one.

stats.label: Maximum fine under the EU’s Digital Services Act
stats.note: The EU can fine large platforms up to this share of global revenue for failing to assess and mitigate content risks.
stats.detail: The duty applies to platforms with more than 45 million monthly EU users (about 10% of the EU’s population). The Commission’s published list of designated very large platforms and search engines includes Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and Google Search. It is the most developed working example of a duty-of-care model as an alternative to the US liability-shield approach.

stats.label: Views of platform power · Pew, 2024
stats.note: 83% of Americans say platforms intentionally censor viewpoints; 78% say social media has too much power in politics; 51% favor more regulation of tech.
stats.detail: Perceived censorship is high on both sides, but only one side moved: 74% of Democrats say platforms intentionally censor viewpoints they object to, up from 66% in 2022, while Republicans have held steady at 93%; the overall share rose from 77% to 83%. Support for more regulation is more partisan (60% of Democrats, 45% of Republicans), showing concern about platform power is broad even where the preferred remedy is not.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, Americans’ Views of Technology Companies

stats.label: Supreme Court votes in recent platform-speech rulings · 2024–2025

series.label: FSC v. Paxton
series.source_label: Oyez, Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton (2025)

stats.note: Recent Supreme Court rulings left the core questions open: whether curated feeds are the platform’s own speech, and how far state pressure can go.
stats.detail: Moody v. NetChoice (July 1, 2024) unanimously vacated lower-court rulings on Texas and Florida must-carry laws for not properly analyzing the First Amendment questions, leaving both laws blocked without deciding whether moderation itself is protected speech. Murthy v. Missouri (June 26, 2024) dismissed jawboning claims 6-3 for lack of standing rather than ruling on how far government pressure may go. Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton (June 27, 2025) upheld a Texas age-verification law for adult sites 6-3, a precedent age-verification proposals for minors on social media now point to.

stats.label: Teens who say they’re online almost constantly · Pew Research, 2024
stats.note: Nearly half of US teens describe their internet use as almost constant, roughly double the share who said so a decade earlier.
stats.detail: 48% of teens ages 13-17 described their internet use as almost constant in Pew’s 2024 survey of 1,391 US teens, up from 24% in Pew’s 2014-15 fielding. That trendline is the baseline both duty-of-care and speech-maximalist positions cite when arguing about platform design and dependency.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, Teens, Social Media and Technology 2024

stats.label: Teens who use each major platform · Pew Research, 2023
stats.note: Reach varies sharply by platform among 13-to-17-year-olds, shaping where age-gating and duty-of-care rules would land hardest.
stats.detail: The survey polled 1,453 US teens between September and October 2023, and all four figures come from that single fielding. Pew’s December 2024 update kept YouTube near-universal at 90%, while older platforms such as Facebook have continued to lose teen users over the past decade.
stats.source_label: Pew Research Center, Teens, Social Media and Technology 2023

stats.label: People worldwide who use social media · DataReportal, 2026
stats.note: More than two in three people on Earth now use social media monthly, though the count reflects accounts rather than unique individuals.
stats.detail: DataReportal’s April 2026 Global Overview aggregates platform-reported ad-audience figures; duplicate accounts and multi-platform users mean the true number of unique people is lower than the headline figure. The scale is the backdrop for every position in this debate: any rule, whether a liability shield or a duty of care, applies at billions-of-posts-a-day scale.

questions.text: Does moderating lawful-but-harmful content measurably reduce real-world harm, or mostly displace it?
questions.why: Removal counts measure volume, not causation, and banned communities resurface elsewhere, so the same numbers read either as progress or as proof the harm just moved.
questions.detail:
The strongest evidence for real reduction comes from studies of large deplatforming events, where removing a hateful community or account correlated with less of that content spreading network-wide rather than a full migration elsewhere. The strongest evidence for displacement comes from the well-documented flight of banned users and content to smaller, less-moderated platforms and encrypted channels, where it becomes harder to measure but is not obviously gone.

Public-health-oriented reformers point to falling prevalence of specific harm categories, like self-harm content, after policy changes as proof of concept. Free-expression and platform-ecology researchers counter that most studies measure removal, not downstream harm to real people, and that whack-a-mole enforcement mainly pushes bad actors toward platforms with weaker safety infrastructure and less transparency, which could worsen outcomes even as flagship platforms look cleaner.

questions.text: Which is the graver threat to open discourse: concentrated private power over speech, or state power over platforms?
questions.why: Both can shape what a democracy hears, and people weigh a handful of unelected executives against a government holding subpoenas and legal leverage very differently.
questions.detail:
The case for private power as the graver threat rests on scale and opacity: a handful of companies set the practical rules for global political speech, change them unilaterally with no meaningful appeal, and market concentration leaves users nowhere else to go.

The case for state power as the graver threat rests on coercive capacity: government holds tools private companies do not, including the power to jail, fine, subpoena, or regulate a platform into compliance, and informal pressure campaigns can achieve censorship a government could never impose directly and constitutionally. Broad, largely bipartisan public unease about concentrated tech power tends to be steady over time, while concern about state pressure on platforms tends to track whichever party currently controls government and feels its own speech was targeted.

questions.text: Would narrowing or repealing Section 230 curb harm, or trigger over-removal of lawful speech and entrench incumbents?
questions.why: Critics on every side blame the same shield for opposite failures: too much harmful content staying up, or too much lawful speech coming down.
questions.detail:
Reform advocates argue that removing the shield for algorithmically amplified or foreseeably harmful content would force platforms to internalize costs they currently externalize onto users, particularly minors, and would end an unusually broad immunity most other industries and most other countries do not extend to distributors.

Legal scholars and civil liberties groups counter that litigation exposure without the shield would push platforms toward defensive over-moderation, since removing speech is cheaper than defending it in court, and that only the largest incumbents could absorb the resulting compliance and litigation costs, entrenching the very concentration critics decry. Most First Amendment and internet-law scholarship on comparable liability regimes leans toward the over-removal and entrenchment prediction, even as political appetite for repeal remains bipartisan and largely untethered from that scholarship.

questions.text: Is a ranked feed the platform’s own protected speech, or infrastructure that can be made to carry all comers?
questions.why: The same ranking algorithm reads as a newspaper choosing its front page or as a phone line that cannot refuse a call, depending on which analogy wins.
questions.detail:
The editorial-speech view holds that ranking, recommending, and removing content are inherently expressive choices, no different in kind from a newspaper’s front page, and that forcing a platform to carry content it has ranked down or removed is compelled speech.

The common-carrier view holds that dominant platforms function as essential infrastructure for public discourse the way telephone networks or utilities do, and that their market power and self-description as open, neutral platforms justify treating the pipe differently from the content flowing through it. Recent appellate and Supreme Court rulings have leaned toward recognizing at least some algorithmic curation as protected expressive activity, while leaving room for narrower transparency or process rules that stop short of dictating specific editorial outcomes, so the doctrine is still being worked out case by case rather than settled.

questions.text: Can minors be walled off from harmful content without identity checks that end online anonymity for everyone?
questions.why: Every age-gating method on offer checks an ID, infers age from behavior, or pushes the check onto app stores and devices, and each narrows anonymous access for adults too.
questions.detail:
Child-safety advocates argue some friction is unavoidable and acceptable: age assurance can be layered and privacy-preserving, using on-device estimation or third-party attestation rather than handing platforms a government ID, and the harm of leaving minors unprotected outweighs a modest reduction in adult anonymity.

Digital-rights and security researchers counter that every age-verification method deployed at real scale so far has either required identity documents, created new data-breach targets, or relied on biometric estimation with real error rates and bias, and that shifting verification to app stores or devices moves the identity chokepoint rather than removing it. The privacy-preserving cryptographic approaches proponents cite, like zero-knowledge age proofs, remain largely unproven under the scale and adversarial conditions a major platform actually faces, which is why most technologists still treat the anonymity trade-off as real rather than solved.

questions.text: Where does legitimate government persuasion of platforms end and unconstitutional coercion begin?
questions.why: From outside the room the same official email reads as routine public-health outreach or as a veiled threat, depending on who sent it and what leverage they held.
questions.detail:
Those defending robust government contact with platforms point out that officials have always flagged fraud, foreign disinformation, and imminent-harm content, and that treating all such contact as coercive would blind government to genuine threats it is uniquely positioned to spot.

Jawboning hawks point to documented episodes combining content requests with explicit or implied threats of antitrust action, regulation, or liability reform, arguing the legal test should turn on whether a reasonable platform executive would perceive a threat, not on whether the government used the word demand. Courts have so far struggled to draw a clean line: recent litigation over pandemic-era and election-related contact between agencies and platforms was resolved largely on procedural standing grounds rather than a substantive coercion standard, leaving the underlying boundary essentially undecided and highly fact-dependent case by case.

questions.text: Do transparency reports, appeals, and user-choice tools actually restore trust, or merely add process?
questions.why: Platforms have run appeals and published transparency reports for years; the fight is whether that machinery changes outcomes or just documents the same contested calls in more detail.
questions.detail:
Proponents of procedural reform point to research on procedural justice showing people accept an adverse decision far more readily when they believe the process was fair and they had a chance to be heard, and note that internal and third-party oversight bodies have in fact reversed a meaningful share of the decisions they review.

Skeptics point out that transparency reports mostly report volume rather than accuracy or consistency, that appeal systems are frequently automated, slow, or effectively unreachable at the scale of billions of daily moderation decisions, and that user-choice filtering tools shift the burden of managing platform-scale harm onto individual users rather than fixing the underlying decisions. The most consistent finding across independent audits of these systems is that they improve perceived fairness for the users who successfully navigate them, without much evidence yet that they meaningfully change the volume or consistency of contested removals at scale.

positions.name: Duty-of-Care Reformer
positions.steelman: Platforms knew the harm and shipped it anyway: the law should make them answer for it.
positions.description: Every other industry that mass-manufactures products used by children, cars, toys, drugs, answers to a duty-of-care standard when its design choices foreseeably cause harm; platforms should be no exception. Recommendation algorithms, autoplay, infinite scroll and streaks are not neutral pipes carrying other people’s speech, they are engagement features a company builds, tests and tunes. CDC survey data show the share of US teen girls reporting persistent sadness or hopelessness rose from 36% in 2011 to 57% in 2021, and Meta’s own leaked research told the company Instagram was worsening body-image and suicidal-ideation problems for a meaningful share of teen girls while it sat on the findings. A company that knows its product foreseeably harms a class of users and chooses growth over redesign has failed a duty of care, and the law, not the company’s discretion, should say so.
positions.detail:
The modern push traces to Frances Haugen’s 2021 disclosure of internal Meta research, reported by the Wall Street Journal as the “Facebook Files,” showing the company’s own researchers had found Instagram made body-image and suicidal-ideation problems worse for a share of teen girls, and that leadership knew. Senators Richard Blumenthal and Marsha Blackburn introduced the Kids Online Safety Act months later; it passed the Senate 91-3 in July 2024 but stalled in the House. In June 2026 the House instead passed a rival package, the Kids Internet and Digital Safety (KIDS) Act, H.R. 7757, by 267-117: it folds in pieces of KOSA but drops the duty-of-care standard, adds mandatory age verification, and preempts some state child-safety laws. KOSA’s Senate authors did not take the trade, and on August 5, 2026 the Senate Commerce Committee advanced KOSA by voice vote with the duty of care intact, a fight proponents describe as ongoing, not lost. The UK moved further and faster: its Online Safety Act 2023 imposes a statutory duty of care enforced by Ofcom, with fines up to £18 million or 10% of global turnover, a model partly forged in the case of Molly Russell, a 14-year-old whose 2017 death a coroner later found had been contributed to by self-harm content she was algorithmically shown; her father Ian Russell now chairs the Molly Rose Foundation.

The legally decisive move has been reframing the claim from speech to product. Lawyers like Matthew Bergman of the Social Media Victims Law Center, representing school districts and bereaved families against Meta, TikTok, Snap and Google, argue the defect is not any user’s post but the addictive architecture itself, infinite scroll, autoplay, variable-reward notifications, deliberately engineered to maximize time on app, the same negligent-design theory used against carmakers and drug manufacturers. A 2023 lawsuit by 33 state attorneys general plus DC against Meta leans on the company’s own suppressed research to make the same point: the harm was foreseen, documented internally, and shipped anyway. Reformers debate tactics among themselves, some favor the UK/EU model of mandated risk assessments and regulator oversight, others want a private right of action so enforcement doesn’t depend on a regulator’s appetite, but the underlying claim is shared.

Proponents concede the free-speech objection is the one to take seriously, and answer it by insisting the target is design, not expression: default settings, notification cadence, and what the ranking algorithm amplifies, not what any user is permitted to say. They point out that minors have always carried narrower legal protections than adults, curfews, ratings, sales-age laws, precisely because judgment and impulse control differ by age, and argue a platform that profiles a 13-year-old and serves her the content most likely to keep her scrolling is exercising the same kind of design power a car dealer or toy maker never gets to wave away with a speech defense.
positions.proponents: Frances Haugen, Jonathan Haidt, Sen. Richard Blumenthal, Sen. Marsha Blackburn, Matthew Bergman (Social Media Victims Law Center), Fairplay, American Psychological Association, Ian Russell / Molly Rose Foundation, Baroness Beeban Kidron / 5Rights Foundation
positions.representative_note: Meta product manager turned whistleblower whose 2021 disclosure of internal research, and testimony that Instagram’s own teams knew of harms to teen girls, catalyzed the Kids Online Safety Act, the UK Online Safety Act’s child-safety duties, and the EU Digital Services Act’s risk-assessment regime.

positions.name: Speech Maximalist
positions.steelman: The cure for bad speech is more speech, not a censor’s veto over what’s lawful.
positions.description: Speech should be met with more speech: the state and dominant platforms alike should stay out of policing what is merely unpopular, offensive, or wrong once it clears the line of actual illegality (true threats, incitement, fraud, child sexual abuse material). That line already exists in law; “lawful but harmful” has no fixed edge, so it becomes a license for whoever holds the button to suppress disfavored views under a rotating label. Mike Masnick’s “impossibility theorem” makes the practical case: at billions of posts a day, even 99.9 percent accuracy still produces millions of wrongful calls, so there is no well-moderated equilibrium, only a choice of which errors to prefer. The sounder default is minimal removal plus maximal user control: keep Section 230’s shield so intermediaries are not forced to over-remove out of legal fear, and let counter-speech, labeling, blocklists and community notes do the work censorship cannot do without silencing the innocent.
positions.detail:
The lineage runs from Mill’s On Liberty through Justice Brandeis’s concurrence in Whitney v. California: “the remedy to be applied is more speech, not enforced silence.” American free-expression maximalism has always drawn a sharp line between illegal speech (narrow, defined categories: true threats, incitement to imminent violence, fraud, CSAM) and merely harmful speech (broad, contested, a moving target: disinformation, hate speech, self-harm content). Section 230 was written in 1996 precisely to keep platforms out of that second, undefined territory, letting them moderate at their own discretion without becoming liable as publishers for everything they leave up.

There is a real fault line inside the camp: absolutists like Elon Musk favor “anything legal stays, full stop,” while civil libertarians such as Nadine Strossen (former ACLU president, author of “HATE: Why We Should Resist It With Free Speech, Not Censorship”) argue for narrow, viewpoint-neutral carve-outs plus aggressive counter-speech and education, not blanket permissiveness. What unites them is skepticism that “harmful but lawful” can be enforced fairly. Masnick’s theorem is the sharpest version of that skepticism: apply a filter with a 99.9 percent accuracy rate to billions of daily posts and the false-positive count alone runs into the millions, meaning any mandate to remove more “harmful” content is also a mandate to censor more true, legal speech, not just more bad speech.

Jacob Mchangama’s Future of Free Speech project tracks a global retreat on this front: broadly written online-harms and hate-speech statutes outside the US have increasingly swept up satire, protest speech, and minority political viewpoints along with their intended targets, the predictable result of asking platforms or regulators to police a category with no stable definition. The proponents’ conclusion is not that platforms should do nothing: transparency, appeals, and user-side filtering tools are welcome. It is that removal mandates for lawful content, whether imposed by governments or induced by liability fear, treat the symptom (bad speech persists somewhere) by cutting into the cure (more speech, freely contested).
positions.proponents: Mike Masnick, Jacob Mchangama, Nadine Strossen, Greg Lukianoff, Ken White, Electronic Frontier Foundation
positions.representative_note: Techdirt founder; “Masnick’s Impossibility Theorem” (2019) argues content moderation at internet scale can never be done well, only chosen among trade-offs between under- and over-removal.

positions.name: Harm-Accountability Advocate
positions.steelman: Amplified hate is a business choice, not free speech: make the company answer for it.
positions.description: Refusing to amplify hate is not censorship, it is the ordinary editorial duty of any publisher, and the First Amendment restrains government, not the content policies of private companies. What platforms defend as speech is really a set of ranking, recommendation and ad-targeting decisions that make hate and lies profitable, with the cost falling on the communities they target rather than on the company. Meta made the point itself in January 2025, ending US third-party fact-checking and loosening its hateful-conduct rules the moment the political weather changed, which is roughly what a voluntary standard is worth. So the lever has to come from outside the boardroom: research that documents the amplification, advertisers who decline to fund it, and civil-rights standards written into policy instead of left to a CEO’s discretion.
positions.detail:
The organizing model predates the current fight. Change the Terms launched in 2018, co-led by Free Press alongside Color of Change, the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law, the National Hispanic Media Coalition and the Southern Poverty Law Center, and wrote model corporate policies on hateful activity that more than 60 organizations have since endorsed: not a law, a standard platforms could be held to by the people who use and advertise on them. Stop Hate for Profit followed in July 2020, when the ADL, the NAACP, Color of Change, Free Press, Common Sense and Sleeping Giants persuaded more than a thousand advertisers to pause their Facebook spending for a month over the company’s handling of hate and voter suppression. Free Press states the constitutional premise plainly: “The First Amendment doesn’t apply to the policies of private companies; it applies only to government actions.”

The evidence arm is research that measures amplification rather than volume. The Center for Countering Digital Hate, founded by Imran Ahmed, publishes studies tracing how recommendation systems serve eating-disorder, self-harm and extremist material to new accounts, and its 2024 STAR framework, Safety by Design, Transparency, Accountability and Responsibility, sets out what the camp wants in policy terms, including liability tied to amplification rather than to hosting. GLAAD’s annual Social Media Safety Index grades platforms on LGBTQ safety, and the ADL’s annual survey measures how much online harassment lands on which groups. The counter-pressure is part of the record too: X Corp. sued CCDH in 2023 over its research and a federal judge dismissed the case in March 2024, finding the suit was about punishing the defendants for their speech, while the advertising industry’s Global Alliance for Responsible Media shut down in August 2024 days after X sued it, which proponents read as confirmation that coordinated advertiser standards were working.

The camp argues among itself over the lever. One wing wants enforcement to stay in civil society and the market, on the view that pressure from researchers, advertisers and users is itself protected speech and carries none of the state-coercion risk free-expression groups warn about. Another wants the EU route, binding systemic-risk assessments and audits, on the view that Meta’s January 2025 rollback proved a standard nobody can enforce is not a standard at all. Both answer the censorship charge the same way: none of this bars a person from speaking, it decides what a company will spend to spread, and a firm that sells amplification is making a business decision its users, its advertisers and eventually its regulators are entitled to price.
positions.proponents: Free Press and the Change the Terms coalition, Imran Ahmed and the Center for Countering Digital Hate, Anti-Defamation League, Color of Change, GLAAD, NAACP, Common Sense Media
positions.representative_note: A civil-rights coalition co-led by Free Press whose model corporate policies on hateful activity, endorsed by more than 60 organizations, rest on the premise that the First Amendment restrains government, not the content policies of private companies.

positions.name: Due-Process Reformer
positions.steelman: Moderate all you want, but show your work and give users a real appeal.
positions.description: Platforms have every right to set and enforce their own rules: the problem was never that they moderate, it’s that for years they did it in secret, with no notice, no stated reason, and no appeal. Due process doesn’t require a platform to carry content it doesn’t want; it requires the basic fairness owed to anyone facing a sanction: name the rule that was broken, offer a real chance to contest the call, and publish the aggregate numbers so outsiders can check for bias or overreach. The EU’s Digital Services Act already requires large platforms to give a stated reason for every removal, log it in a public database, and offer an independent out-of-court reviewer, and Meta’s own Oversight Board overturned the company’s original call in roughly seven of every ten of its earliest cases. Mandate the process, not the outcome, and legitimacy follows.
positions.detail:
The position has a paper trail longer than most: the Santa Clara Principles began in 2018 out of the Content Moderation at Scale conferences, when a coalition of civil-liberties groups (EFF, ACLU, Access Now, Article 19, CDT) sat down with platforms and wrote down what fair process should look like, numbers on enforcement actions taken, notice to affected users, and a meaningful path to appeal. The 2021 update, Principles 2.0, followed consultation with more than 50 organizations and added foundational commitments on human rights, cultural competence, and transparency about state requests. That the current text is endorsed by Meta, Google, Reddit, Apple, GitHub, and X is itself the argument: this is the rare speech position that has already won substantial buy-in from the companies it constrains, not a demand shouted from outside.

The Oversight Board is the position’s most-watched experiment and its most contested one. Funded through an irrevocable trust to insulate it from Meta’s ordinary chain of command, it hears a small number of hard cases and can order individual posts reinstated, decisions Meta is bound to follow. Legal scholar Evelyn Douek noted its early rulings “strike at matters fundamental to the way Facebook designs its content moderation system,” not a rubber stamp. It draws fire from both directions, which reformers take as a sign it’s doing something real: critics on the left built a shadow “Real Facebook Oversight Board” doubting its independence, while Senator Josh Hawley called it “a special censorship committee.” Kate Klonick, who got embedded access to document its creation, frames bodies like this as the emergence of “New Governors,” private actors doing a public job that badly needs public-style scrutiny.

The frontier is turning appeal rights into infrastructure rather than platform goodwill. The DSA’s Article 17 to 21 machinery, statement-of-reasons filings, internal complaint handling, and certified out-of-court dispute settlement, now applies across the EU’s roughly 450 million users regardless of which platform they’re on, with a growing roster of certified reviewer bodies operating across the EU. Stanford’s Francis Fukuyama has pushed the logic one step further with “middleware”: let users choose their own third-party ranking and filtering layer on top of a platform’s content, turning the appeal from a one-off grievance process into standing user control. Daphne Keller, who spent years as Google’s associate general counsel before moving to Stanford’s Cyber Policy Center, is the position’s sharpest internal critic of overreach in the other direction, warning that mandates can just as easily entrench incumbents who can afford the compliance apparatus. That’s the position’s core wager: it doesn’t ask who gets to decide what stays up, only that the exercise of that power be visible, explained, and contestable.
positions.proponents: Kate Klonick, Evelyn Douek, Daphne Keller, Francis Fukuyama, Electronic Frontier Foundation, Access Now, ACLU, Meta’s Oversight Board
positions.representative_note: The founding text of this position: a coalition-drafted transparency and appeals standard endorsed by Meta, Google, X, Reddit, Apple, and GitHub, since given legal teeth by the EU’s Digital Services Act.

positions.name: Common-Carrier Regulator
positions.steelman: Dominant platforms are the modern public square; no boardroom gets to pick who’s let in.
positions.description: Social media is not just another business, it is the modern public square, and a business that holds itself open to everyone has never gotten to pick and choose whose speech it carries. That is the settled logic of common-carrier law: telegraph lines, phone networks and railroads all earned duties of nondiscriminatory service once they became the essential channel the public had to pass through, and today’s platforms meet that same test. Facebook and YouTube alone already reach 38 percent and 35 percent of US adults for news, a concentration of gatekeeping power no electorate voted to create and no user can appeal. Justice Clarence Thomas laid out the case in his 2021 Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute concurrence: platforms with this kind of near-utility control over speech look far more like the common carriers the law has always regulated than like a newspaper hand-picking op-eds, so courts and legislatures, not terms of service, should set the rules for who gets carried.
positions.detail:
Common carriage is centuries old: English law bound innkeepers, ferrymen, and other common callings to serve all comers, because refusal by the sole route through a bottleneck was a public harm, not just a private choice. American law carried that duty into canals, railroads, telegraph, and telephone as each became the essential channel of its era, from Munn v. Illinois (1877) through the interstate framework that later governed AT&T. Legal scholars Adrian Vermeule, Philip Hamburger, and Adam Candeub revived the doctrine for the platform era starting around 2020, arguing that Facebook, YouTube, and Twitter meet every historical trigger for carrier status: they hold themselves open to the public indiscriminately, they dominate an essential communications channel, and a user cut off has no real substitute.

The doctrine gained judicial traction fast. Justice Thomas’s 2021 concurrence in Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute is the movement’s founding text, and the Fifth Circuit picked up the thread in NetChoice v. Paxton (2022): Judge Andrew Oldham upheld Texas HB 20’s ban on viewpoint-based deplatforming, writing bluntly that the platforms’ editorial choices are censorship, not speech the First Amendment protects. That split hard with the Eleventh Circuit, which struck down Florida’s parallel SB 7072 as compelled speech, and the Supreme Court’s 2024 Moody v. NetChoice ruling vacated both decisions on procedural grounds without resolving the common-carrier question itself, remanding it rather than rejecting it. Proponents read that silence as the fight staying open, not lost, and must-carry bills keep moving through state legislatures.

The strongest evidentiary hook is Packingham v. North Carolina (2017), where the Supreme Court itself called social media the modern public square, the place a citizen goes to petition, debate, and hear from elected officials. If the Court will strike down a law that walls a citizen out of that square, proponents ask, why should a private company’s terms of service be allowed to do the same thing to millions at once? The camp is not fully united on how far the duty should reach: Volokh has pushed a narrower, purely viewpoint-neutral must-carry rule to avoid handing government broader speech-control tools, while others favor sweeping structural mandates modeled on telephone-style common carriage. But all agree that a company screening billions of posts by algorithm is nothing like a newspaper hand-selecting op-eds, and it should not get to claim the same editorial-discretion shield.
positions.proponents: Clarence Thomas, Adrian Vermeule, Philip Hamburger, Adam Candeub, Eugene Volokh, Andrew Oldham, Josh Hawley
positions.representative_name: Justice Clarence Thomas — Biden v. Knight First Amendment Institute concurrence (2021)
positions.representative_note: The movement’s founding legal text: platforms with this much concentrated control over the public square forfeit unlimited editorial discretion and should be regulated as common carriers, not treated as newspapers.

positions.name: Jawboning Hawk
positions.steelman: Government pressure on platforms is censorship laundered through a private middleman.
positions.description: The First Amendment restrains government, not Meta or X, so when an agency leans on a platform with regulatory threats, subpoenas, or a sustained pressure campaign to pull lawful posts, that is state censorship wearing a corporate mask, whichever party is doing the leaning. Bantam Books v. Sullivan settled in 1963 that informal government pressure can violate the First Amendment as surely as a formal ban: the test is coercion, not whether the order came on letterhead. The Fifth Circuit found exactly that pattern in Missouri v. Murthy, ruling that FBI, CDC and White House officials had coerced or significantly encouraged platforms to remove Covid and election content, before the Supreme Court dismissed the case on standing alone in June 2024 without reaching the merits. Weeks earlier the same Court ruled unanimously for the NRA against a New York regulator who pressured banks and insurers to cut the group off, with the ACLU itself as the NRA’s lawyer: a structural check on state power, not a partisan grievance.
positions.detail:
The paper trail starts with the Twitter Files, internal records Elon Musk released to journalists Matt Taibbi, Bari Weiss, Michael Shellenberger, David Zweig, and Lee Fang between December 2022 and March 2023. They showed the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force routinely flagging accounts to Twitter’s Trust and Safety team, White House staff requesting tweet takedowns, and CDC officials weighing in on Covid moderation calls. Missouri and Louisiana, joined by individual plaintiffs including Jay Bhattacharya and Martin Kulldorff and represented by the New Civil Liberties Alliance’s Jenin Younes, sued in 2022 as Missouri v. Biden, alleging a coordinated federal pressure campaign against disfavored viewpoints. The case became Murthy v. Missouri at the Supreme Court.

The doctrinal fight turns on the line between persuasion and coercion. Judge Terry Doughty’s 2023 injunction found the government “used its power to silence the opposition”; the Fifth Circuit narrowed but largely upheld that finding, citing officials’ own emails threatening “fewer legal protections” and warning platforms they were “hiding the ball.” The Supreme Court’s 6-3 majority, written by Justice Barrett in June 2024, threw the case out for lack of standing, citing “a dearth of facts” tying any specific plaintiff’s removal to government action; Justice Alito’s dissent, joined by Thomas and Gorsuch, argued the majority looked away from “one of the most important free speech cases” in decades. That leaves the merits question open rather than resolved.

The cross-partisan proof point is NRA v. Vullo, decided unanimously weeks before Murthy: a Democratic New York financial regulator who pressured banks and insurers to drop the NRA after Parkland lost 9-0, with Justice Sotomayor writing that officials “cannot attempt to coerce private parties in order to punish or suppress views that the government disfavors,” and with the ACLU’s David Cole arguing the NRA’s side. The Knight First Amendment Institute’s jawboning tracker catalogues pressure campaigns from officials of both parties on that same premise. Hawks debate among themselves how far the principle should cut: Jacob Mchangama and others warn that state must-carry and hate-speech mandates aimed at platforms are jawboning’s regulatory cousin, and that a movement which only flags pressure from the opposing party isn’t defending a principle at all.
positions.proponents: Jenin Younes and the New Civil Liberties Alliance, Jacob Mchangama (Future of Free Speech), Matt Taibbi and the Twitter Files journalists (Michael Shellenberger, Bari Weiss, David Zweig), the Knight First Amendment Institute’s Jawboning Project, the Missouri and Louisiana attorneys general in Missouri v. Murthy
positions.representative_name: Knight First Amendment Institute’s Jawboning Litigation Tracker
positions.representative_note: An academic project cataloging jawboning suits against officials of both parties, from NRA v. Vullo (a Democratic New York regulator) to Missouri v. Murthy (the Biden White House), on the premise that the coercion problem is structural, not partisan.

crux.lead: If someone has to hold the veto over lawful speech, whose hands scare you least?
crux.subtitle: Six camps that cannot agree on the danger: five fear a different hand on the veto, one says the harm left standing is the damage, and every remedy is someone’s nightmare.
crux.empirical: Testable in principle: does moderating lawful-but-harmful content reduce real-world harm or displace it; would narrowing the liability shield curb abuse or trigger over-removal while entrenching the incumbents who can afford compliance; do transparency and appeals change outcomes or add process; can minors be gated without identity checks for everyone.
crux.values: Evidence can’t rank the fears. Whether concentrated private power or state power is the graver threat to open discourse, whether a ranked feed is the platform’s own speech or infrastructure owed to all comers, and where persuasion of platforms shades into coercion are judgments about who, if anyone, may hold a veto over lawful speech.

actions.title: Back Fairplay’s campaigns
actions.description: Fairplay pushes platforms and lawmakers, including through the Kids Online Safety Act, to design for child safety over engagement.

actions.title: Learn why EFF defends Section 230
actions.description: EFF lays out why the liability shield keeps user speech online and what narrowing or repealing it would break.

actions.title: Read Free Press on platform accountability
actions.description: Free Press and its Change the Terms coalition set out model policies on hateful activity, and why they call this private governance rather than censorship.

actions.title: Read the Santa Clara Principles
actions.description: A coalition-backed standard, endorsed by major platforms, for moderation transparency, notice, and real appeals.

actions.title: Track the must-carry case
actions.description: SCOTUSblog’s case file follows Moody v. NetChoice, the still-unresolved fight over Texas and Florida laws barring platforms from removing users by viewpoint.

actions.title: Back the New Civil Liberties Alliance
actions.description: The New Civil Liberties Alliance litigates against government pressure on platforms to moderate lawful speech, including in Murthy v. Missouri.

actions.title: Support the ACLU’s speech work
actions.description: ACLU campaigns against decency mandates and age-verification rules it says thin out lawful speech online.

actions.title: Back the age-appropriate design push
actions.description: 5Rights Foundation’s petition calls for binding design standards that make platforms safe for kids by default.

actions.title: Back CCDH’s STAR framework
actions.description: The Center for Countering Digital Hate’s blueprint for safety by design, transparency, accountability for amplification, and independent research access.

notes: Web search could not be run for the missing-camp check (session search budget exhausted), so camp coverage was assessed from existing knowledge of the field. On that basis the six camps cover the genuinely active positions: child-safety/duty-of-care, speech maximalist, proceduralist, common-carrier right, jawboning hawks, and the civil-rights/harm-accountability left, and each is steelmanned in its own voice with real named proponents and its internal fault lines acknowledged, which is a strong parity signal.

Closest call on omission: the decentralization/'protocols not platforms' camp (Masnick's protocols essay, Bluesky/fediverse, Fukuyama's middleware) is distributed across other camps rather than named — Masnick fronts Speech Maximalist and middleware appears inside Due-Process Reformer's detail. Its answer to the title question ('nobody decides centrally; users pick their own moderation layer') is distinct enough that a one-line acknowledgment in scope_covered or the Due-Process detail would close the gap cleanly. Not blocking because its actual proponents are all represented.

Question 2 detail ends by characterizing concern about private power as 'steady' and concern about state pressure as tracking 'whichever party currently controls government' — a subtle asymmetry that mildly delegitimizes the state-power-threat side as partisan-motivated, in a question whose whole point is that the two fears are weighed differently in good faith. Consider either sourcing that claim or cutting the sentence; the Jawboning Hawk section itself documents the cross-partisan counterexample (NRA v. Vullo).

Question 3 detail: 'political appetite for repeal remains bipartisan and largely untethered from that scholarship' — reporting the scholarship lean is legitimate honest non-balance, but 'untethered' editorializes against repeal advocates. A flatter phrasing ('repeal advocates dispute or discount that prediction') carries the same information without the jab.

Actions asymmetry: five camps get advocacy-flavored actions (donate/policy/learn-more at an aligned org) while Common-Carrier Regulator's sole action is a neutral SCOTUSblog case tracker. If an appropriate advocacy or scholarship link exists (e.g. a Volokh/Candeub explainer), parity would improve; minor because the tracker is still on-side.

The platform-industry status-quo voice (NetChoice, CCIA, trade groups arguing current private moderation plus Section 230 works fine) never appears as its own camp and is the implicit defendant in every position's narrative; its policy substance is essentially covered by Speech Maximalist plus Due-Process Reformer, so this is acceptable, but a strong published topic might name that overlap explicitly in one of those two details.

Speech Maximalist: the description's opening claim that 'the state and dominant platforms alike should stay out of policing what is merely unpopular' does not fit the named representative. Mike Masnick and EFF emphatically defend platforms' right to moderate at their own discretion (that is the point of their Section 230 advocacy); their target is mandates and liability-induced over-removal, not platform moderation itself. The detail paragraph and the closing lines ('transparency, appeals, and user-side filtering tools are welcome') correct this, and the internal Musk-vs-Strossen fault line is acknowledged, so a proponent would endorse the section overall — but tightening the opening to target removal mandates rather than platform discretion would make Masnick's endorsement unreserved.

The platform-industry position itself (NetChoice/CCIA: moderation is our protected editorial speech, Section 230 works as designed, leave the current regime alone) has no dedicated section. Its substance is distributed across Speech Maximalist, Due-Process Reformer, and the 'platform's speech' question, so no major argument is actually missing, but a reader may notice the parties with the most at stake have no camp of their own. Worth a deliberate editorial call rather than an accident.

Duty-of-Care Reformer is the strongest steelman in the set: it leads with the proponents' best evidence (internal research, CDC trendline, product-design framing), names its own tactical disagreements, and answers the speech objection the way real proponents do. Harm-Accountability Advocate, the position most often strawmanned elsewhere, is likewise given its genuine strongest case (amplification-as-business-decision, the Vullo-style distinction between private and state pressure implied via 'First Amendment restrains government'), including honest treatment of the Meta 2025 rollback as their own proof point.

Jawboning Hawk earns cross-partisan credibility with NRA v. Vullo and the Knight tracker as representative, which is exactly how the strongest proponents (Mchangama, Knight Institute) frame it; a movement-partisan version would have been weaker. No change needed.

Common-Carrier Regulator: a real proponent would endorse it, including the honest Volokh-vs-structural split. One small strengthening option: proponents often add the network-effects/lock-in economic argument (no exit means no market discipline), which appears only in the crux question detail, not in the position itself.

blocking.issue: why_now overstates the legal holding. It says juries held Meta liable in March 2026 "despite Section 230 defenses, cracking the shield that has defined online speech law for thirty years." The two March 2026 verdicts are real and correctly dated (K.G.M. v. Meta, Los Angeles Superior Court jury, Meta and Google/YouTube liable; New Mexico v. Meta, state-court jury, consumer-protection violations and enabling child exploitation, ~$375m + $372m in penalties). But Meta raised Section 230 and the defense was NOT adjudicated in either decision — the record is that the claim "was not considered in both decisions," with the shield question expected to surface only on appeal. No court cracked the shield; the verdicts simply routed around it on a product-design theory.
blocking.fix: Rewrite to what actually happened, e.g.: "In March 2026 juries in Los Angeles and New Mexico held Meta liable for design and algorithm harms on a product-defect theory that never reached its Section 230 defense, teeing up the shield's first real test on appeal." Keeps the hook, drops the unearned holding.

blocking.issue: Tier-1 Basics stat "6% of global revenue" is sourced to a page that does not contain the figure. The cited URL (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/digital-services-act-package) loads fine and does support the 45-million-user threshold, but a full-text check found no mention of any maximum fine percentage anywhere on it — its only penalty reference is the €550m AliExpress fine. The 6% cap is correct on the merits (Art. 74(1), Regulation (EU) 2022/2065), but the headline number is not on the cited page.
blocking.fix: Repoint source_url to a page that states the cap — the EUR-Lex text of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 Article 74 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32022R2065) — or keep the package page as source and move the 6% support to a Commission Q&A page that states it. Update source_published/source_accessed to match.

blocking.issue: Both DSA point-in-time counts are wrong and stale. (a) Basics stat 4 detail: "records 26 services as of August 2026, 25 of them currently in scope after Stripchat's designation was terminated in May 2025." The Commission's designated-VLOP/VLOSE list (page last updated 24 July 2026) carries roughly 28-31 designated services, not 26 — the figure appears to be a 2024-era snapshot. The "25 in scope" arithmetic is also wrong: Stripchat's designation was terminated 27 May 2025 and obligations ceased four months later, so it is not among current designations and should not be netted out of an August 2026 count. (b) Due-Process Reformer detail: "nine certified reviewer bodies already operating" — the Commission's Article 21 out-of-court dispute settlement page (updated 2 July 2026) lists 11 certified bodies. Both are exactly the kind of perishable roster count this atlas is supposed to avoid, sitting next to durable structural figures that already carry the point.
blocking.fix: Preferred: drop both counts. Stat 4's detail already has the durable facts it needs (45m-user threshold ≈ 10% of EU population, named platforms in scope, most developed duty-of-care model), and the Due-Process detail is just as strong as "a growing roster of certified out-of-court reviewer bodies now operating across the EU." If a count is kept, recount both against the Commission pages as of the access date and state the as-of date inline, accepting they will need re-checking every refresh.

blocking.issue: Spliced quotation attributed to Justice Brandeis. Speech Maximalist detail renders the Whitney v. California concurrence as: "the fitting remedy for evil counsels is good ones, not enforced silence." Those are two separate sentences from two different paragraphs. Brandeis wrote "the fitting remedy for evil counsels is good ones" in one passage, and "If there be time to expose through discussion the falsehood and fallacies, to avert the evil by the processes of education, the remedy to be applied is more speech, not enforced silence" in another. Presenting the join inside one set of quotation marks is a misquotation of a canonical source.
blocking.fix: Quote one or the other. Cleanest: "...through Justice Brandeis's concurrence in Whitney v. California: the remedy to be applied is more speech, not enforced silence." Or keep "the fitting remedy for evil counsels is good ones" and end the quotation there.

notes: VERIFIED CLEAN (no action needed): Pew 2024 tech-companies stat matches the source exactly — 83% overall (up from 77% in 2022), 93% Republicans, 74% Democrats (up from 66% in 2022), 78% too much political power, 51% favor more regulation (60% D / 45% R). Pew teens 2024: 48% almost constantly, up from 24%, n=1,391, fielded Sept 18-Oct 10 2024. Pew teens 2023: TikTok 63 / Snapchat 60 / Instagram 59, n=1,453, Sept 26-Oct 23 2023. DataReportal: 5.79bn user identities, April 2026, 'more than 2 in 3 people', accounts-not-individuals caveat all verbatim-accurate. NERA 2017: 425,000 jobs and $44bn confirmed. Section 230 carve-out list confirmed. Facebook 38% / YouTube 35% for news confirmed against Pew's social-media-and-news fact sheet (fielded Aug 18-24, 2025). Court votes and dates all correct: Moody 9-0 July 1 2024 (docket 22-277), Murthy 6-3 June 26 2024 (23-411), FSC v. Paxton 6-3 June 27 2025 (23-1122) — Oyez docket paths in the draft are correct. Barrett's 'dearth of facts' confirmed. KIDS Act confirmed: H.R. 7757, passed House June 29 2026 by 267-117, drops KOSA's duty of care, adds age verification, preempts certain state child-safety laws. KOSA Senate 91-3 on July 30 2024 confirmed. Santa Clara Principles confirmed: began 2018 out of the Content Moderation at Scale conferences, 2.0 after consultation with 50+ organizations, endorsed by Apple, Meta, Google, Reddit, Twitter/X, GitHub. CCDH STAR framework confirmed (Sept 19 2024; 'consequences for harmful content algorithmically amplified or monetized'). Stripchat termination date (27 May 2025) confirmed. DSA 45m threshold ≈10% of EU population and 6% cap both correct on the merits.

The Aug 5, 2026 Senate Commerce claim is half-confirmed and worth a human check before publish. The committee site does show an Aug 5, 2026 executive session and a Cantwell opening statement 'at Markup of Kids Online Safety Bills', so the event is real and correctly dated. What I could not independently confirm is the specific characterization — 'advanced KOSA by voice vote with the duty of care intact'. Nothing contradicts it, but it is a one-week-old procedural detail doing real work in the Duty-of-Care position (it is what makes the fight 'ongoing, not lost'). Confirm the vote method and whether the reported text retained the duty of care.

Oversight Board overturn rate: 'roughly seven of every ten cases it decided in its earliest rulings' is soft. The one precisely checkable early anchor is the first tranche (Jan 28, 2021): five cases, four overturned — 80%. ~70% is a defensible characterization of the early cumulative rate and is widely reported, but since this number is carrying the evidentiary weight of the steelman ('evidence that the underlying decisions were often simply wrong'), consider anchoring it to a specific tranche, e.g. 'overturned Meta in four of its first five rulings.'

CDC teen-girls figure is accurate as written (36% in 2011 to 57% in 2021) and properly dated, but 2021 is now the peak rather than the latest reading — the 2023 YRBS put female students reporting persistent sadness or hopelessness at 53%. A reader could take 57% as current. Consider a four-word parenthetical ('easing slightly to 53% by 2023') so the trend claim survives the next refresh without a reader feeling misled.

Pew censorship measure loses a word. Pew's item is 'social media sites intentionally censor political viewpoints they find objectionable'; the draft's series label and detail both drop 'political' ('censor viewpoints they find objectionable' / 'viewpoints they object to'). Same-measure precision — restore 'political' in both places.

Alito paraphrase drifts one notch. He called Murthy 'one of the most important free speech cases to reach this Court in years'; the draft quotes the fragment accurately but completes it outside the quotation marks as 'in decades'. Change to 'in years' to match.

Pew 2023 YouTube figure: the report's prose says 'roughly nine-in-ten', and the draft's 93% headline comes from the topline table (with the Dec 2024 update at 90%, which the draft correctly distinguishes). The three sibling figures all matched exactly, so the source is right; just worth a glance at the topline PDF to confirm 93% rather than 92% before publish.

nclalegal.org/take-action/ returned 403 to automated fetching — almost certainly bot blocking rather than a dead link (the domain is live), but it is the one action URL I could not confirm renders. Worth a manual browser check. The other action links I tested all load and support their descriptions: 5rightsfoundation.com/eaca/en-eu/ (a real petition for binding design standards, four demands, correctly characterized) and the CCDH STAR framework page.
verdicts.post_run_fixes_applied: All 4 blocking issues fixed per the critic's prescriptions before persisting (2026-08-12): why_now legal-holding rewrite; DSA 6% cap re-sourced to EUR-Lex Art. 74; both perishable roster counts dropped; Brandeis quotation unspliced.

notes: The subtitle's tally ("five name a different captor of lawful speech, one says the harm left standing is the damage") arguably misassigns the Duty-of-Care Reformer: that camp's own steelman ("Platforms knew the harm and shipped it anyway") is a harm-first diagnosis, explicitly disclaiming speech as its target ("the target is design, not expression"), so the honest count is closer to four captor-naming camps and two harm-first camps (Duty-of-Care and Harm-Accountability). The lead's axis still works for all six, and no position's substance is distorted, so this is polish, not a blocker — but sharpening to "four … two" (or a formulation that avoids the count entirely, e.g. "camps that cannot even agree whether the danger is who holds the veto or what the feed leaves standing") would make the subtitle strictly accurate.

The lead does real narrowing work: "Every fix for the feed hands power to someone — so whose hands scare you least?" locates the live disagreement at trust allocation over speech power rather than at "is harm real," and every camp can answer it in its own voice (courts, users, process, legislatures, no-one-in-government, civil society/advertisers). No house verdict, no both-sides mush, no binary compression of a six-camp field.

The empirical/values split is clean and matches the questions section: the empirical paragraph lists genuinely testable claims (displacement, over-removal, process outcomes, age-gating), and the values paragraph correctly frames the fear-ranking, speech-vs-infrastructure, and persuasion-vs-coercion questions as judgments evidence cannot settle. "Evidence can’t rank the fears" is a strong, neutral bridge line.

Above-fold picture is sound: the four T1 stats (shield's age, public sentiment, SCOTUS votes, DSA fine) plus the four T1 questions and all six steelmen give a correct map of the debate without needing any detail field; no load-bearing caveat lives only below the fold.

Stat 3 (SCOTUS votes): headline value 9-0 is only Moody, but the wide ranked series shows all three vote counts and the note explicitly says the rulings left the core questions open, which prevents the false 'settled law' reading. Good compact hygiene.

Jargon: 'jawboning' first appears above the fold cold, in the Murthy series label ('dismissed jawboning claims for lack of standing'), before any definition; the Jawboning Hawk steelman defines the concept only implicitly. A reader scanning Basics first meets an unexplained term of art. Consider rewording the series label to 'dismissed government-pressure claims' or similar (presentation-only change).

Q4 text uses a straight ASCII apostrophe ('platform's own protected speech') where every other content field uses curly; typographic-punctuation rule violation in an above-fold compact field. Fix: replace with ’ in questions[3].text (fold preview shows the same in the crux/preview line).

Crux subtitle says 'one says the harm left standing is the damage', but two camps fit that description (Duty-of-Care Reformer and Harm-Accountability Advocate both argue the standing harm is the injury); the five-vs-one split is arguable. Not misleading enough to block, but worth a second look.

Denominator scope, minor: stats 5 and 6 are labeled 'Teens' without the US qualifier (values are % of US teens 13-17); the notes say 'US teens' / the details clarify, and both are below the fold, so acceptable, but adding 'US' to the labels would be tighter.

Stat 7 label 'People worldwide who use social media' sits in slight tension with the value's true denominator (accounts, not unique people); the unit string 'billion accounts' and the note's caveat resolve it in the compact layer, so no mislead survives.
questions[5].lean_pct_a is -1 (presumably a 'no lean shown' sentinel for the T2 jawboning question); confirm the renderer treats it as hidden rather than drawing a negative bar.

blocking.issue: BASICS stat "Supreme Court votes in recent platform-speech rulings" (T1, above fold), series[2] label: "Murthy v. Missouri (dismissed jawboning claims for lack of standing)" uses "jawboning" as bare jargon in a compact field. This is the first place a reader meets the word, before the Jawboning Hawk position card defines it, and the stat's note does not gloss it either. Fails the zero-unexplained-jargon bar for the compact register.
blocking.fix: Reword that series label only, keeping the case name and outcome intact: "Murthy v. Missouri (dismissed claims of government pressure on platforms, for lack of standing)". No fact changes: same case, same disposition.

blocking.issue: ACTIONS item "Back NCLA's jawboning fight" (T1, condensed): the compact title stacks a bare acronym (NCLA, never expanded anywhere in the action, the description also opens with bare "NCLA") on top of the same unexplained jargon ("jawboning"). A smart general reader scanning action cards gets neither word.
blocking.fix: Retitle to "Back the fight against government pressure" (or "Back the New Civil Liberties Alliance") and open the description with the expanded name: "The New Civil Liberties Alliance litigates against government pressure on platforms to moderate lawful speech, including in Murthy v. Missouri." Same org, same fact set, same url.

notes: Overall the draft holds the compact/expanded split well: every stat detail genuinely adds figures, methodology, or caveats over its note (e.g. the Pew censorship stat's partisan breakdown, the DataReportal accounts-vs-people caveat), and no question detail merely restates its why. No restatement flags.

Stat 1 detail: "the DMCA" is a bare acronym in the expanded register with no first-use definition. Suggest "...Section 230 and the DMCA (copyright's safe-harbor law)...". Note-level since expanded readers tolerate more, but the register rules ask for definition at first use.

Stat 3 series labels also carry "vacated" and "lack of standing": legal terms of art, though common in news coverage, and the stat's note does translate the upshot in plain language. Acceptable at parity; "threw out lower rulings" would be plainer for Moody if edited anyway.

Position name "Jawboning Hawk" is jargon, but its steelman ("Government pressure on platforms is censorship laundered through a private middleman") defines the concept immediately below the name, and question 6's text/why cover the same ground jargon-free. Acceptable as-is; no change needed once the two blocking instances are fixed, since the position card then becomes the reader's first proper introduction.

Cross-dimension observation (typography, not reading level): several straight ASCII apostrophes survive in content fields, e.g. question 4 text ("the platform's own protected speech"), its lean label "Platform's speech", action titles "Back Fairplay's campaigns" and "Support the ACLU's speech work", and the Jawboning Hawk proponents/representative_name ("Knight First Amendment Institute's"). House rule requires curly apostrophes; flagging for whichever critic owns punctuation.

Crux subtitle runs three clauses in one sentence and is the densest compact line in the draft; it parses on a second read and the lead above it is excellent, so note-level only. A lighter cut: "Six camps, five fearing a different hand on the veto, one insisting the harm left standing is the damage."
Compact numbers are consistently retainable: "more than two in three people on Earth", "nearly half... roughly double a decade earlier", "30 years". Good calibration against the example bar.

BASICS tiering is sound: the four T1 stats map one-to-one onto the topic's structural core (the liability shield's age, public sentiment on platform power, the open SCOTUS doctrine, and the DSA as the working duty-of-care alternative), and the drop to teen-usage context stats at T2 is a genuine importance drop-off. Global-accounts backdrop at T3 is correctly the least decision-relevant.

QUESTIONS T1 set is the right four: each anchors a major fault line (displacement evidence, private vs state power, Section 230 reform, feed-as-speech), and the last directly serves the why_now (Moody left it open). Boundary at T2 is defensible.

Mild asymmetry worth knowing about, not fixing: the transparency/appeals question sits at T3 while its companion position (Due-Process Reformer, prevalence 15, T1) is above the fold. Questions and positions need not mirror, and the process question is genuinely the least gripping of the seven, but if the human ever wants tighter coupling, swapping it with the T2 jawboning question would pair each below-fold question with a below-median-prevalence position. Current arrangement is within parity.

Similarly, the jawboning question at T2 while Jawboning Hawk is T1 is acceptable: all six positions render above the fold by design (6/6), so every position's companion question cannot also be T1 with only four slots.
POSITIONS: 6/6 above the fold in real prevalence order; no promotion/demotion issue possible on this dimension.

plan_positions.name: Duty-of-Care Reformer
plan_positions.sketch: Platforms design for engagement and profit from foreseeable harm; the law should make them answer for it, especially where minors are concerned.

plan_positions.name: Speech Maximalist
plan_positions.sketch: Lawful speech stays up: the cure for bad speech is more speech, and moderation beyond illegality is censorship by another name.

plan_positions.name: Due-Process Reformer
plan_positions.sketch: Private moderation is legitimate; opaque, unappealable moderation is not — mandate transparency, appeals, and user-controlled filters.

plan_positions.name: Common-Carrier Regulator
plan_positions.sketch: Dominant platforms are the modern public square; law, not corporate discretion, should bar viewpoint discrimination in what they carry.

plan_positions.name: Jawboning Hawk
plan_positions.sketch: The real censor is the state working through platforms; police government pressure on moderation no matter which party holds power.
